title: Guardrail Erosion in Domain Fine-Tuned Large Language Models: A Paired Audit of Knowledge-Centric Abstention in Biomedical LLMs
content:
Computer Science > Computation and Language

Title:Guardrail Erosion in Domain Fine-Tuned Large Language Models: A Paired Audit of Knowledge-Centric Abstention in Biomedical LLMs
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:The number of domain fine-tuned models, particularly in the biomedical domain, is rapidly expanding. Fine-tuning promises high-performing models at a fraction of the cost of training a base model, but it can also produce unintended behavioral changes. Multiple studies have shown that safety guardrails can erode with fine-tuning, yet large-scale studies across model architectures, data mixtures, and fine-tuning methodologies remain limited. Where prior work in this space has studied value-centric refusal, this work focuses on knowledge-centric abstention. We audit 25 biomedical domain fine-tuned large language models against 11 paired base checkpoints on MedAbstain and ClinDet-Bench to evaluate the impact of fine-tuning on knowledge-centric abstention. We find that defined appropriate abstention measured by these benchmarks, already low in base models (median 8.3% on MedAbstain), falls further after fine-tuning (median 4.2%, decreasing in 21 of 25 pairs on MedAbstain), and that the magnitude and direction of change are heterogeneous across pairs. These results motivate fine-tuning methods that improve domain-specific capability while preserving appropriate caution.

report.summary: A paired audit finds biomedical fine-tuning often reduces LLMs’ willingness to abstain when uncertain, with appropriate abstention falling in 21 of 25 model pairs.
report.background: Domain fine-tuned models are expanding rapidly, especially in biomedicine, because fine-tuning can deliver specialized performance at far lower cost than training a base model. But fine-tuning can also cause unintended behavioral shifts. Prior work has documented erosion of safety guardrails, often focused on value-centric refusal—whether a model refuses harmful requests. This study examines a different concern: knowledge-centric abstention, or whether a model appropriately declines to answer when it lacks reliable knowledge. Large-scale evidence across architectures, data mixtures, and fine-tuning methods remains limited. The authors conduct a paired audit of 25 biomedical fine-tuned LLMs against 11 base checkpoints using MedAbstain and ClinDet-Bench to isolate fine-tuning’s effects on appropriate caution.
key_points: The study uses a paired audit design: 25 biomedical domain fine-tuned LLMs are compared with 11 paired base checkpoints on two benchmarks, MedAbstain and ClinDet-Bench. Pairing models helps isolate changes caused by fine-tuning rather than differences in base architecture or scale.

Appropriate abstention is already low in base models: the median was 8.3% on MedAbstain. After biomedical fine-tuning, the median fell to 4.2%, and abstention decreased in 21 of 25 paired comparisons, suggesting fine-tuning often makes models less willing to withhold uncertain answers.

The direction and size of change are heterogeneous across model pairs. Not every fine-tuned model loses caution to the same degree, and some may behave differently. This means the risk cannot be inferred from domain or method alone; each fine-tuning pipeline needs its own audit.

The findings connect domain specialization with calibration risk. Fine-tuning for biomedical knowledge can improve task performance while weakening the model’s ability to recognize knowledge limits, motivating training methods that preserve appropriate abstention alongside domain capability.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the results argue that domain fine-tuning should include abstention and calibration audits, not just accuracy benchmarks. Model releases and model cards should report paired base-versus-fine-tuned comparisons, especially in high-stakes fields. Developers should test whether fine-tuning reduces uncertainty signaling and add regression checks before deployment. For regular users, biomedical chatbots may become more fluent and confident after specialization while becoming less likely to say “I don’t know,” increasing misinformation risk. The effect is heterogeneous, so blanket assumptions are unsafe. Safer practice requires explicit abstention evaluations, uncertainty-aware interfaces, and human oversight for clinical or health-related use.
report.tools: Watch MedAbstain and ClinDet-Bench for knowledge-centric abstention evaluation; Hugging Face for paired checkpoints and model cards; PEFT/LoRA, Axolotl, and Unsloth for fine-tuning experiments; and lm-evaluation-harness or custom paired-audit scripts for regression testing. Combine these with calibration and uncertainty libraries, plus human-review workflows for biomedical deployments.
